strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation spanning seven diverse subsurface benchmarks (faulted CO2 storage, Cartesian hydrocarbon extraction, radial wastewater injection, 3D nested LGR basin-scale CO2 storage, and 3D dynamic-mesh ATES), covering structured, unstructured, nested, and dynamically-adapting meshes — a genuinely broad and application-relevant test suite.

The core architectural idea — fusing a Perceiver-style global cross-attention branch with a local GNO branch via a learned per-location gate, then feeding fused tokens to DiT-style blocks with temporal/scalar conditioning — is a sensible and reasonably well-motivated way to capture both long-range pressure propagation and short-range heterogeneity in subsurface fields.

The ablation experiments (global-only vs local-only vs fused) are included for nearly every benchmark and consistently show the fused variant improving over either single-branch variant, supporting the paper's central architectural claim.

The demonstration of direct training on Dynamic-Mesh-Optimization (time-varying topology) data without interpolation is a distinctive and practically useful capability that most competing neural operators (fixed-grid CNN/FNO, or graph nets requiring constant topology) cannot offer.

Cross-dataset training (Section 4.3) and OOD generalization to unseen geostatistical facies (Section 4.2) are useful additional experiments that speak to the paper's stated ambition of a subsurface foundation-model backbone.

Reproducibility details are unusually thorough: architecture hyperparameters, optimizer settings, training time/memory, and dataset generation protocols are documented at length in the appendix for every benchmark.
weaknesses: No code or trained models are available at submission ("will be released upon publication"), and several datasets are newly created by the authors (ATES, Channelized LGR, OOD wastewater); independent verification of the central claims is currently impossible.

On the CarBench benchmark, APT does *not* achieve the best R^2/Rel-L2 among the 11 compared models (it ranks second per Table 13), which sits awkwardly with the abstract's blanket claim that "APT outperforms SOTA architectures ... across both regular and irregular grids." The authors also admit they reproduced the baseline protocol themselves rather than using released code/splits, and observed larger variance and missing test cases, weakening the fairness/validity of this specific comparison.

The abstract advertises "robust super-resolution capabilities," but Section 4.1 shows APT actually degrades by 1.8% at full resolution on the ATES dataset, with the text conceding this reflects insufficient mesh convergence in training data rather than a strength; the claim of robustness is therefore overstated relative to the more nuanced discussion in the body.

The method is largely a careful integration of existing components (Perceiver cross-attention, radius-graph GNO pooling, DiT-style adaptive modulation, learned gating fusion) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the novelty is primarily in the specific combination and its application to adaptive/dynamic subsurface meshes, which is a valid but comparatively modest form of originality.

Hyperparameters (supernode counts, latent token counts, hidden dims, optimizers) are tuned separately and substantially differently per dataset (e.g., Lion optimizer with wd=0.5 in one case, AdamW wd=1e-4 in another; token counts ranging from 128 to 1024), raising the possibility that per-dataset tuning inflates reported gains and makes it harder to assess a single "backbone" design's true generality.

Baseline parameter counts are inconsistently matched across tables (sometimes APT is much smaller, e.g., 12M vs 33M on hydrocarbon; sometimes comparable), and for several tables only 1-2 baseline families (U-Net/FNO or MGN/MGN-LSTM) are compared, without a graph-based or interpolation-free baseline for every adaptive-mesh setting (e.g., ATES only compares to interpolated grid baselines, no adapted GNN baseline despite GNNs being highlighted elsewhere as the natural competitor for irregular/dynamic meshes).

No analysis of physical consistency/conservation properties (mass, energy) of predictions is provided, which is an important consideration for subsurface flow/heat-transport surrogates intended for decision-critical applications like GCS or ATES.

All evaluation is on synthetic/simulated data; no real-field validation is attempted or discussed as a limitation, and the Impact Statement is generic without deeper discussion of risks of surrogate misuse (e.g., overconfidence in unseen geological regimes) for safety-critical applications such as CO2 storage integrity or induced seismicity from wastewater injection.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important and underexplored problem: learning neural surrogates that can handle the intrinsic spatial heterogeneity and adaptive/unstructured mesh topologies characteristic of subsurface systems, going beyond the homogeneous-domain assumption of prior physics transformers (UPT, Transolver).

Very broad experimental scope spanning seven benchmarks (2D irregular fault mesh, Cartesian hydrocarbon, radial wastewater, 3D nested LGR, 3D dynamic-mesh ATES, OOD geostatistics, cross-dataset training), which is unusually comprehensive for a methods paper.

The claim of being able to train directly on Dynamic Mesh Optimization (time-varying topology/node count) outputs without interpolation is a genuinely useful capability, and the ATES experiment (Table 3) demonstrates a concrete, non-trivial advantage over grid-interpolated baselines.

The ablation studies (fused vs. global-only vs. local-only) are included in essentially every benchmark and consistently support the core architectural claim that combining local and global branches helps, which is good methodological hygiene.

The discussion of super-resolution limits (Section 4.1) is commendably honest: the authors explicitly caution that super-resolution claims should not be overstated when training data itself is not mesh-converged, rather than spinning the ATES degradation as a success.
Extensive appendix with governing equations, dataset generation protocols, and training hyperparameters for every benchmark, which aids reproducibility more than the truncated main text alone.
weaknesses: Several of the most novel-sounding claims (adaptive-mesh learning, OOD generalization, cross-dataset/foundation-model training) are evaluated exclusively on datasets created by the authors themselves (ATES-DMO subset processing, Channelized LGR dataset, OOD Gaussian/von-Karman split) with no independent baselines from the literature beyond FNO/U-Net variants reimplemented by the authors; this makes it hard for outside readers to verify the difficulty/realism of these settings or compare against future work.

The authors explicitly acknowledge in Appendix C.1.4 that their CarBench comparison numbers differ from the official codebase/protocol due to un-released sampling scripts and reproduced testing splits, and that this contributes to abnormally large variance in their results; on this exact benchmark APT does not achieve the best R² (ranks second), which undercuts the abstract's blanket claim that APT 'outperforms SOTA architectures... across both regular and irregular grids.'

The core architectural novelty (gated fusion of a global Perceiver branch and a local GNO branch) is explicitly acknowledged by the authors to closely resemble prior hybrid neural operators (Wen et al. 2022; Liu & Tang 2025; Liu-Schiaffini et al. 2024); the differentiation offered ('used to construct latent tokens rather than as a decoding mechanism') is a fairly narrow architectural distinction rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

No code or data is released at submission time ("will be released upon publication"), so none of the seven benchmark pipelines, custom datasets, or training configurations can currently be independently verified, which is a meaningful reproducibility gap given how central the custom datasets are to several headline claims.

Comparisons are not uniformly fair in terms of compute budget: inference speedups are reported prominently (e.g., 4902×, 6800× over classical simulators), but training cost/compute relative to baseline ML models is inconsistently reported, and some baselines (e.g., Nested FNO with 682M parameters vs. APT's 17.9M) are compared primarily on accuracy/parameter count without controlling for training data or iterations, making some 'wins' partly a function of architecture search rather than a controlled ablation.

Some benchmarks use fairly small or narrow test sets (e.g., 200 test samples on a 40×40 grid for the hydrocarbon benchmark, single held-out configuration for CarBench qualitative figures), limiting the statistical strength of the reported superiority claims.

The paper's writing in the main text compresses substantial architectural detail (positional encoding scheme, gating parameterization, decoder cross-attention stacking choices) into the appendix, making the main-text methodology section hard to fully assess without cross-referencing many appendix subsections.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: learning directly from adaptive/dynamically-refined meshes (DMO, LGR) without interpolation, which is a meaningful practical contribution for subsurface simulation where mesh topology varies over time or across simulation instances.

Broad and diverse empirical evaluation spanning five to seven benchmarks covering structured, unstructured, nested, and dynamically-adaptive meshes, and multiple physical regimes (single/multiphase flow, heat transport, compositional CO2 storage), which stress-tests generality more than most neural operator papers.

The fused local-global architecture (Perceiver-style global cross-attention + local GNO branch with a learned gate) is a reasonable and well-motivated design for subsurface heterogeneity, and the paper backs the design with ablations (global-only vs local-only vs fused) across multiple datasets that consistently favor the fused variant.

Strong quantitative improvements over relevant baselines (MGN-LSTM, U-FNO, Nested FNO, U-Net) with substantial parameter reduction (e.g., 97% fewer parameters than Nested FNO with comparable accuracy) and large inference speedups over commercial/open-source simulators.

Reasonably thorough appendix with governing equations, dataset generation protocols, hyperparameters, training costs (memory, throughput, wall-clock), and evaluation metric definitions, supporting reproducibility for readers who wish to replicate the numerical setups.

Honest and nuanced discussion of super-resolution limitations, explicitly distinguishing architecture mesh-invariance from data-driven mesh-convergence bounds, and forthrightly reporting a case (CarBench) where APT is not the top performer and explaining discrepancies from the official baseline codebase.
weaknesses: Several of the paper's most novel claims (learning from DMO adaptive meshes, cross-dataset/foundation-model-style training, OOD robustness) are evaluated only on newly created, author-generated datasets without established community benchmarks or independent verification, and in some cases (e.g., Table 6 cross-dataset training) there is no comparison against any competing method attempting the same task—only an internal ablation—so the 'first to enable X' claims are not contrasted against alternatives that might partially achieve similar behavior with workarounds.

On the one dataset with the widest baseline comparison (CarBench, 11 competing methods), APT is not the best performer by R² (ranks second) even though it is emphasized as state-of-the-art elsewhere; the text attributes larger variance to protocol/reproduction discrepancies from an unreleased official codebase, which is a plausible but unverifiable explanation and slightly weakens confidence in the fairness of comparisons on that benchmark.

The core architectural novelty (gated fusion of local and global branches) is incremental relative to cited prior gated hybrid neural operators (Wen et al. 2022; Liu & Tang 2025; Liu-Schiaffini et al. 2024); the differentiation—using the fusion to construct a latent token space rather than as a decoding mechanism—is a relatively modest conceptual shift rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Code and datasets are not yet released (promised only upon publication), so external verification of the extensive empirical claims across seven benchmarks is currently not possible, which is a meaningful reproducibility gap for a paper whose primary contribution is empirical/architectural rather than theoretical.

Some experimental settings mix custom baseline adaptations (e.g., U-Net/FNO trained on interpolated grids, MGN retrained with noise injection tricks from prior work) which, combined with the use of author-curated datasets for the most novel claims, introduces a risk of benchmark and comparison design favoring the proposed method that is not fully mitigated by the ablations shown.

The efficiency narrative is somewhat one-sided: while inference speedups are dramatic, training costs (up to tens of GB of GPU memory and tens of minutes to nearly an hour per epoch for the larger 3D datasets, as shown in Table 7) are non-trivial and are not compared against baseline training costs, making it hard to assess the net computational trade-off of adopting APT for large-scale pretraining as advocated in the discussion.

strengths: Extremely comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning five diverse subsurface benchmarks (irregular faulted PEBI meshes, Cartesian grids, HR-adaptive DMO meshes, million-cell nested LGR meshes, and a newly created channelized reservoir dataset), covering structured, unstructured, and dynamically adaptive mesh topologies.

The fused local-global gated encoder is a sensible and well-motivated architectural contribution for subsurface systems with sharp local heterogeneity (permeability contrasts, fault interfaces) combined with long-range pressure propagation; ablations (global-only vs local-only vs fused) consistently show the fusion mechanism improves accuracy across nearly all benchmarks, which is convincing evidence for the core design choice.

APT is demonstrated to learn directly from HR-adaptive (dynamic mesh optimization) simulation data with time-varying mesh topology, a genuinely novel capability that most competing mesh-native architectures (MGN, Transolver, MINO) cannot handle (MINO runs OOM on the ATES dataset).

Cross-dataset training experiment (Section 4.4) convincingly shows that APT's mesh-agnostic design enables joint training across datasets with incompatible LGR structures, substantially boosting performance on a data-limited task (R2 32.0%→86.7%), supporting the foundation-model framing.

Honest and nuanced discussion of super-resolution limitations (Section 4.1), correctly distinguishing architectural mesh-invariance from the fundamental data-fidelity ceiling imposed by simulation mesh convergence, rather than overselling zero-shot super-resolution claims.

Extensive appendix with governing equations, training/hyperparameter details, computational cost tables, and additional visualizations supports reproducibility of the described experiments, and an added evaluation on standard homogeneous PDE benchmarks (Airfoil, Darcy, Elasticity) probes generality beyond the subsurface domain.
weaknesses: On the standard homogeneous PDE benchmarks (Table 17) APT is consistently second-best, trailing Transolver on every dataset, which somewhat undercuts the implicit claim that the fused local-global design is broadly superior rather than specifically tuned/beneficial for heterogeneous subsurface data.

Several benchmarks (ATES, wastewater injection with OOD split, channelized LGR dataset) are newly created by the authors rather than public/independently validated; combined with the statement that code and data will only be released "upon publication," this limits independent verification of the simulation setups and results at review time.

Many key comparisons lack statistical rigor: no error bars or multiple-seed reporting for several central tables (e.g., Table 4 basin-scale LGR results, Table 6 cross-dataset results, Table 7 scaling results), and the CarBench super-resolution comparison in Table 5 (top) is based on a single representative test sample rather than the full test set, weakening the strength of some headline claims.

The architecture itself is a combination of largely existing components (Perceiver cross-attention, graph neural operator local pooling, gated fusion, DiT-style modulation blocks); the technical novelty is primarily in the specific combination and its application to subsurface heterogeneity rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

In the basin-scale LGR benchmark (Table 4), Nested-FNO achieves notably better saturation error (1.79% vs. 2.5%) than APT despite using far more parameters; this trade-off is acknowledged but somewhat softened in the framing, and it is unclear how consistently APT's parameter efficiency translates to accuracy advantages versus specialized cascaded baselines.

Baseline tuning effort is not always clearly matched across methods (e.g., differing optimizer/hyperparameter choices, and MINO's inherent memory scaling issue is used to argue APT's advantage without a clear discussion of whether MINO could be adapted with sparse/chunked attention), raising some concern about comparison fairness.

strengths: Extremely comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning five main benchmarks (faulted CO2 storage, Cartesian hydrocarbon, adaptive-mesh ATES, basin-scale LGR CO2 storage) plus additional created datasets for OOD generalization, cross-dataset training, scaling behavior, and standard homogeneous PDE benchmarks (Airfoil/Darcy/Elasticity) in the appendix.

The architectural motivation (spatial heterogeneity in subsurface media vs. homogeneous domains assumed by prior physics transformers such as UPT/Transolver) is clearly articulated and reasonably well supported by the local-global gated fusion ablations, which generally show fused variants outperforming local-only or global-only versions.

Demonstrated ability to learn directly on HR-adaptive (dynamic mesh optimization) simulation data with time-varying topology, a genuinely difficult setting where several strong baselines (MGN, MINO) fail outright due to fixed-topology or memory constraints.

Extensive reproducibility details in the appendix (architecture hyperparameters, training costs, GPU memory/throughput tables, dataset generation protocols, governing equations) that would materially aid reproduction.

The super-resolution discussion (Section 4.1) is commendably honest, explicitly cautioning that super-resolution claims are bounded by training-data mesh convergence rather than overselling architectural mesh-invariance.
weaknesses: Several of the benchmark datasets used to demonstrate superiority (Channelized LGR dataset, Wastewater/OOD dataset) are created by the authors specifically for this paper, which limits independent verifiability of the comparisons and raises concern about implicit tuning advantages for APT over baselines that were not co-developed with these datasets.

Superiority over prior SOTA is not uniform: in Table 4, Nested-FNO still achieves better saturation error (1.79% vs 2.5%) despite APT's parameter efficiency, and in several tables the ablated GNO/local-only variant is already very close to or competitive with the fused model (e.g., Table 1 local-only delta-Sg=0.36 vs fused 0.32), somewhat undercutting the claimed necessity of the fusion mechanism.

The architectural contribution is largely a recombination of existing components (Perceiver cross-attention, GNO/radius graph pooling, DiT-style modulation, gated fusion used elsewhere as a decoding mechanism) repositioned to construct latent tokens; the novelty is incremental rather than a fundamentally new operator-learning principle.

Some headline claims (e.g., 'first architecture to learn directly from HR-adaptive mesh refinement simulations') rest on the fact that competing methods (MGN-family) are architecturally incapable of handling changing topology by design, making the comparison somewhat definitional rather than a demonstration of a technical breakthrough over methods designed for a different problem class.

Table 5's CarBench super-resolution comparison reports results for only a single representative test sample rather than an aggregate over the test set, which is a weak statistical basis for the claimed mesh-convergent behavior, especially given how central this claim is to the discussion section.

Hyperparameter/tuning parity between APT and baselines is not clearly established; baseline models (Transolver, UPT, MINO, HOOD) appear to be run largely with default or lightly adjusted configurations while APT benefits from dataset-specific architectural tuning (e.g., varying supernode counts, radius, latent tokens per dataset), raising fairness concerns in the comparisons.

The paper is a very long, dense combination of many disparate experiments; the incremental contribution per experiment (scaling behavior, cross-dataset training with only two datasets, OOD generalization) is each fairly thin and could individually be seen as insufficient to support the broad foundation-model-backbone framing claimed in the abstract and conclusion.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and underexplored problem: existing physics-transformer neural operators (UPT, Transolver) assume domain homogeneity and are ill-suited to the intrinsic multi-scale heterogeneity of subsurface systems (permeability contrasts, fault interfaces, sharp saturation fronts). The proposed local-global gated fusion directly targets this gap with a clear mechanistic rationale (integral vs. differential operator inductive biases).

Exceptionally broad and diverse empirical validation: five core subsurface benchmarks spanning structured, unstructured, nested, and fully HR-adaptive (dynamic mesh optimization) meshes, plus additional studies on super-resolution, OOD generalization to unseen geostatistical fields, cross-dataset joint training, scaling behavior, and even three standard homogeneous PDE benchmarks (Darcy, Airfoil, Elasticity) for generality.

Consistent and controlled ablations (fused vs. local-only vs. global-only, and w/ vs. w/o fusion) across nearly every experiment convincingly isolate the contribution of the fusion mechanism, rather than relying on aggregate comparisons alone.

APT is demonstrated to be the first model able to learn directly from HR-adaptive (time-varying topology) mesh data (ATES dataset), a genuine capability gap relative to MeshGraphNet-style and grid-based methods, with quantitative evidence that MGN/MINO fail or run out of memory on this setting.

Efficiency analysis (Pareto frontier of accuracy vs. inference time/memory, Table 4/Table 11/Table 13 speedups) and detailed appendix reporting per-dataset training cost, hyperparameters, and hardware make the empirical claims well substantiated and largely reproducible in spirit.

The cross-dataset training result (Table 6), while based on a modest dataset size, is a compelling proof-of-concept for the paper's central motivating claim about enabling subsurface foundation models by combining heterogeneous mesh datasets that prior architectures cannot jointly ingest.

The discussion section is unusually candid about the limits of the super-resolution claim (bounded by simulation mesh convergence rather than architecture), which is a mark of scientific honesty rather than a weakness.
weaknesses: Code and datasets are stated as 'released upon publication' rather than provided with submission, and several datasets (ATES, Channelized, Wastewater OOD) are newly created by the authors; reproducibility of the exact benchmark data and their potential selection to favor APT cannot currently be independently verified.

The core architectural novelty (gated fusion of local and global branches) is explicitly acknowledged to already exist in prior hybrid operators (Wen et al. 2022; Liu & Tang 2025; Liu-Schiaffini et al. 2024); the contribution is repositioning the gate to construct the latent token space rather than as a decoding step, which is a comparatively incremental architectural change relative to the scope of claims made in the abstract/introduction.

On the three standard homogeneous-domain PDE benchmarks (Table 17), APT is consistently second to Transolver, suggesting that APT's advantages are largely confined to the heterogeneous subsurface regime rather than being a generally superior architecture, which somewhat tempers the 'physics-agnostic backbone' framing.

Some baseline comparisons rely on previously published checkpoints (e.g., Nested FNO) or on reported numbers from other papers (CarBench baselines) rather than uniformly retrained/tuned baselines under identical compute budgets, making some head-to-head comparisons less tightly controlled than the ablation studies.

Most reported results appear to be single-run point estimates without repeated seeds or confidence intervals (e.g., Tables 3, 4, 6, 7), so the statistical significance of some improvements (e.g., 0.56% vs 0.60% pressure error in Table 2, or marginal gains in Table 15) is not established.

The cross-dataset training experiment, while conceptually important, is demonstrated on a small combined dataset (1,400 samples) and a single train/test configuration; broader validation with more datasets or ablation of what drives the transfer benefit (shared physics vs. shared geometry) would strengthen the foundation-model claim.

The paper's core three-stage formulation (encoder-approximator-decoder) closely follows the general neural-operator/latent-token paradigm established by UPT and Perceiver-IO; the writing sometimes conflates engineering contributions (dataset curation, training recipes) with fundamental architectural novelty.
